{{For|the use of the term in algebraic geometry|Valuation (algebra)}}
In [[geometry]], a '''valuation''' is a finitely additive function from a collection of subsets of a set <math>X</math> to an abelian [[semigroup]]. 
For example, [[Lebesgue measure]] is a valuation on finite unions of [[Convex body|convex bodies]] of <math>\R^n.</math> Other examples of valuations on finite unions of convex bodies of <math>\R^n</math> are [[surface area]], [[mean]] width, and [[Euler characteristic]].

In geometry, [[Continuous function|continuity]] (or [[smoothness]]) conditions are often imposed on valuations, but there are also purely discrete facets of the theory. In fact, the concept of valuation has its origin in the dissection theory of [[polytope]]s and in particular [[Hilbert's third problem]], which has grown into a rich theory reliant on tools from abstract algebra.

==Definition==
Let <math>X</math> be a set, and let <math>\mathcal S</math> be a collection of subsets of <math>X.</math> A function <math>\phi</math> on <math>\mathcal S</math> with values in an abelian semigroup <math>R</math> is called a '''valuation''' if it satisfies 
<math display=block> \phi(A\cup B)+  \phi(A\cap B) = \phi(A) + \phi(B)</math>
whenever <math>A,</math> <math>B,</math> <math>A\cup B,</math> and <math>A\cap B</math> are elements of <math>\mathcal S.</math> 
If <math>\emptyset\in \mathcal S,</math> then one always assumes <math>\phi(\emptyset)=0.</math>

===Examples===
Some common examples of <math>\mathcal S</math> are

* the [[Convex body|convex bodies]] in <math>\R^n</math>
* [[Compact space|compact]] [[Convex polytope|convex polytopes]] in <math>\R^n</math>
* [[Convex cone|convex cones]]
* smooth compact polyhedra in a smooth manifold <math>X</math>


Let <math>\mathcal K(\R^n)</math> be the set of convex bodies in <math>\R^n.</math> Then some valuations on <math>\mathcal K(\R^n)</math> are

* the [[Euler characteristic]] <math>\chi : K(\R^n) \to \Z</math>
* [[Lebesgue measure]] restricted to <math>\mathcal K(\R^n)</math>
* [[Mixed volume#Quermassintegrals|intrinsic volume]] (and, more generally, [[mixed volume]])
* the map <math>A \mapsto h_A,</math> where <math>h_A</math> is the [[support function]] of <math>A</math>


Some other valuations are 
* the lattice point enumerator <math>P \mapsto |\Z^n\cap P|</math>, where <math>P</math> is a lattice polytope
* [[cardinality]], on the family of finite sets

==Valuations on convex bodies==
From here on, let <math>V = \R^n </math>, let <math>\mathcal K(V)</math> be the set of convex bodies in <math>V </math>, and let <math>\phi</math> be a valuation on <math>\mathcal K(V)</math>.

We say <math>\phi</math> is ''translation invariant'' if, for all <math>K \in \mathcal K(V)</math> and <math>x\in V</math>, we have <math>\phi(K+x)=\phi(K)</math>.

Let <math>(K,L) \in \mathcal K(V)^2</math>. The [[Hausdorff distance]] <math>d_H(K,L)</math> is defined as
<math display="block"> d_H(K,L)= \inf\{\varepsilon >0 : K\subset L_\varepsilon \text{ and } L\subset K_\varepsilon \},</math>
where <math>K_\varepsilon</math> is the <math>\varepsilon</math>-neighborhood of <math>K</math> under some Euclidean inner product. Equipped with this metric, <math>\mathcal K(V)</math> is a [[locally compact space]].

The space of continuous, translation-invariant valuations from <math>\mathcal K(V)</math> to <math>\Complex </math> is denoted by <math>\operatorname{Val}(V).</math>

The topology on <math>\operatorname{Val}(V)</math> is the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets of <math>\mathcal K (V).</math> Equipped with the norm 
<math display="block"> \|\phi\| = \max\{ |\phi(K)| : K\subset B\},</math> 
where <math>B\subset V</math> is a bounded subset with nonempty interior, <math>\operatorname{Val}(V)</math> is a [[Banach space]].

===Homogeneous valuations===
A translation-invariant continuous valuation <math>\phi\in \operatorname{Val}(V)</math> is said to be ''<math>i</math>-homogeneous'' if 
<math display=block> \phi(\lambda K)= \lambda^i\phi(K)</math>
for all <math>\lambda>0</math> and <math>K\in \mathcal K(V).</math> The subset <math>\operatorname{Val}_i(V)</math> of <math>i</math>-homogeneous valuations is a vector subspace of <math>\operatorname{Val}(V).</math> [[Peter McMullen|McMullen's]] decomposition theorem<ref name="McMullen">{{citation
| last1=McMullen | first1=Peter | authorlink1=Peter McMullen
| title=Continuous translation-invariant valuations on the space of compact convex sets
| journal=Archiv der Mathematik
| volume=34
| date=1980
| issue=4
| pages=377–384
| doi=10.1007/BF01224974 | s2cid=122127897 | doi-access=}}</ref> states that

<math display=block> \operatorname{Val}(V)= \bigoplus_{i=0}^n \operatorname{Val}_i(V), \qquad n=\dim V.</math>

In particular, the degree of a homogeneous valuation is always an integer between <math>0</math> and <math>n=\operatorname{dim} V.</math>

Valuations are not only graded by the degree of homogeneity, but also by the parity with respect to the reflection through the origin, namely
<math display=block> \operatorname{Val}_i = \operatorname{Val}_i^+ \oplus \operatorname{Val}_i^-,</math> 
where <math>\phi\in \operatorname{Val}_i^\epsilon</math>  with <math>\epsilon \in \{+,-\}</math> if and only if <math>\phi(- K)= \epsilon \phi(K)</math> for all convex bodies <math>K.</math>
The elements of <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^+</math> and <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^-</math> are said to be ''even'' and ''odd'', respectively.

It is a simple fact that <math>\operatorname{Val}_0(V)</math> is <math>1</math>-dimensional and spanned by the Euler characteristic <math>\chi,</math> that is, consists of the constant valuations on <math>\mathcal K(V).</math>

In 1957 [[Hugo Hadwiger|Hadwiger]]<ref name="Hadwiger">{{citation
| last1=Hadwiger | first1=Hugo | authorlink1=Hugo Hadwiger
| title=Vorlesungen über Inhalt, Oberfläche und Isoperimetrie
| publisher=Springer-Verlag
| location=Berlin-Göttingen-Heidelberg
| date=1957
| series=Die Grundlehren der Mathematischen Wissenschaften
| volume=93
| doi=10.1007/978-3-642-94702-5| isbn=978-3-642-94703-2 }}</ref> proved that <math>\operatorname{Val}_n(V)</math> (where <math>n=\dim V</math>) coincides with the <math>1</math>-dimensional space of Lebesgue measures on <math>V.</math>

A valuation <math>\phi\in \operatorname{Val}(\R^n)</math> is ''simple'' if <math>\phi(K)=0</math> for all convex bodies with <math>\dim K<n.</math> [[Rolf Schneider|Schneider]]<ref name="Schneider:Simple">{{citation
| last1=Schneider | first1=Rolf
| title=Simple valuations on convex bodies
| journal=[[Mathematika]]
| volume=43
| date=1996
| issue=1
| pages=32–39
| doi=10.1112/S0025579300011578}}</ref> in 1996 described all simple valuations on <math>\R^n</math>: they are given by <math display=block>\phi(K)=c\operatorname{vol}(K)+\int_{S^{n-1}}f(\theta)d\sigma_K(\theta),</math> where <math>c \in \Complex,</math> <math>f \in C(S^{n-1})</math> is an arbitrary odd function  on the unit sphere <math>S^{n-1}\subset \R^n,</math> and <math>\sigma_K</math> is the surface area measure of <math>K.</math> In particular, any simple valuation is the sum of an <math>n</math>- and an <math>(n-1)</math>-homogeneous valuation. This in turn implies that an <math>i</math>-homogeneous valuation is uniquely determined by its restrictions to all <math>(i+1)</math>-dimensional subspaces.

===Embedding theorems===
The Klain embedding is a linear injection of <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^+(V),</math> the space of even <math>i</math>-homogeneous valuations, into the space of continuous sections of a canonical complex line bundle over the Grassmannian <math>\operatorname{Gr}_i(V)</math> of <math>i</math>-dimensional linear subspaces of <math>V.</math> Its construction is based on Hadwiger's characterization<ref name="Hadwiger" /> of <math>n</math>-homogeneous valuations. If <math>\phi\in \operatorname{Val}_i(V)</math> and <math>E\in \operatorname{Gr}_i(V),</math> then the restriction <math>\phi|_E</math> is an element <math>\operatorname{Val}_i(E),</math> and  by Hadwiger's theorem  it is a Lebesgue measure. 
Hence
<math display=block>\operatorname{Kl}_\phi(E)= \phi|_E</math>
defines a continuous section of the line bundle <math>Dens</math> over <math>\operatorname{Gr}_i(V)</math> with fiber over <math>E</math> equal to the <math>1</math>-dimensional space <math>\operatorname{Dens}(E)</math> of [[Density on a manifold|densities]] (Lebesgue measures) on <math>E.</math>

'''Theorem''' (Klain<ref name="Klain">{{citation
| last1=Klain | first1=Daniel A.
| title=A short proof of Hadwiger's characterization theorem
| journal=[[Mathematika]]
| volume=42
| date=1995
| issue=2
| pages=329–339
| doi=10.1112/S0025579300014625}}</ref>). The linear map <math>\operatorname{Kl} : \operatorname{Val}_i^+(V)\to C(\operatorname{Gr}_i(V),\operatorname{Dens})</math> is injective.

A different injection, known as the Schneider embedding, exists for odd valuations. It is based on Schneider's description of simple valuations.<ref name="Schneider:Simple" /> It is a linear injection of <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^-(V),</math> the space of odd <math>i</math>-homogeneous valuations, into a certain quotient of the space of continuous sections of a line bundle over the partial flag manifold of cooriented pairs <math>(F^i\subset E^{i+1}).</math> Its definition is reminiscent of the Klain embedding, but more involved. Details can be found in.<ref name="Alesker:Book">{{citation
| last1=Alesker | first1=Semyon
| title=Introduction to the theory of valuations
| series=CBMS Regional Conference Series in Mathematics
| volume=126
| publisher=American Mathematical Society
| location=Providence, RI
| date=2018}}</ref>

The Goodey-Weil embedding is a linear injection of <math>\operatorname{Val}_i</math> into the space of distributions on the <math>i</math>-fold product of the <math>(n-1)</math>-dimensional sphere. It is nothing but the [[Schwartz kernel theorem|Schwartz kernel]] of a natural polarization that any <math>\phi\in\operatorname{Val}_k(V)</math> admits, namely as a functional on the <math>k</math>-fold product of <math>C^2(S^{n-1}),</math> the latter space of functions having the geometric meaning of differences of support functions of smooth convex bodies. For details, see.<ref name="Alesker:Book" />

===Irreducibility Theorem===
The classical theorems of Hadwiger, Schneider and McMullen give fairly explicit descriptions of valuations that are homogeneous of degree <math>1,</math> <math>n-1,</math> and <math>n=\operatorname{dim} V.</math> But for degrees <math>1<i<n-1</math> very little was known before the turn of the 21st century. McMullen's conjecture is the statement that the valuations 
<math display=block>\phi_A(K)=\operatorname{vol}_n(K+A), \qquad A\in\mathcal K(V),</math>
span a dense subspace of <math>\operatorname{Val}(V).</math> McMullen's conjecture was confirmed by [[Semyon Alesker|Alesker]] in a much stronger form, which became known as the Irreducibility Theorem:

'''Theorem''' (Alesker<ref name="Alesker:Irred">{{citation
| last1=Alesker | first1=Semyon
| title=Description of translation invariant valuations on convex sets with solution of P. McMullen's conjecture
| journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]]
| volume=11
| year=2001
| issue=2
| pages=244–272
| doi=10.1007/PL00001675 | s2cid=122986474
| doi-access=}}</ref>). For every <math>0\leq i\leq n,</math>  the natural action of <math>GL(V)</math> on the spaces <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^+(V)</math> and <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^-(V)</math> is irreducible.

Here the action of the [[general linear group]] <math>GL(V)</math> on <math>\operatorname{Val}(V)</math> is given by 
<math display=block> (g\cdot \phi)(K)= \phi(g^{-1} K).</math>
The proof of the Irreducibility Theorem is based on the embedding theorems of the previous section and [[Beilinson-Bernstein localization]].

===Smooth valuations===
A valuation <math>\phi\in\operatorname{Val}(V)</math> is called ''smooth'' if the map <math>g\mapsto g\cdot \phi</math> from <math>GL(V)</math> to <math>\operatorname{Val}(V)</math> is smooth. In other words, <math>\phi</math> is smooth if and only if <math>\phi</math> is a smooth vector of the natural representation of <math>GL(V)</math> on <math>\operatorname{Val}(V).</math> The space of smooth valuations <math>\operatorname{Val}^\infty(V)</math> is dense in <math>\operatorname{Val}(V)</math>; it comes equipped with a natural Fréchet-space topology, which is finer than the one induced from <math>\operatorname{Val}(V).</math>

For every (complex-valued) smooth function <math>f</math> on <math>\operatorname{Gr}_i(\R^n),</math>
<math  display="block" >\phi(K)=\int_{\operatorname{Gr}_i(\R^n)} \operatorname{vol}_i(P_E K) f(E) dE,</math>
where <math>P_E : \R^n\to E</math> denotes the orthogonal projection and <math>dE</math> is the [[Haar measure]], defines a smooth even valuation of degree <math>i.</math> It follows from the Irreducibility Theorem, in combination with the Casselman-Wallach theorem, that any smooth even valuation can be represented in this way. Such a representation is sometimes called a ''Crofton formula''.

For any (complex-valued) smooth [[differential form]] <math>\omega\in \Omega^{n-1}(\R^n\times S^{n-1})</math> that is invariant under all the translations <math>(x,u)\mapsto (x+t,u)</math> and every number <math>c\in \Complex,</math> integration over the ''normal cycle'' defines a smooth valuation:
{{NumBlk|:|<math  display="block">  \phi(K)= c\operatorname{vol}_n(K) + \int_{N(K)} \omega, \qquad K\in \mathcal K(\R^n). </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
As a set, the normal cycle <math>N(K)</math> consists of the outward unit normals to <math>K.</math> The Irreducibility Theorem implies that every smooth valuation  is of this form.

==Operations on translation-invariant valuations==
There are several natural operations defined on the subspace of  smooth valuations <math>\operatorname{Val}^\infty(V)\subset \operatorname{Val}(V).</math> The most important one is the product of two smooth valuations. Together with pullback and pushforward, this operation extends to valuations on manifolds.

===Exterior product===
Let <math>V,W</math> be finite-dimensional real vector spaces. 
There exists a bilinear map, called the exterior product, 
<math  display="block">\boxtimes : \operatorname{Val}^\infty(V)\times \operatorname{Val}^\infty(W)\to \operatorname{Val}(V\times W) </math>
which is uniquely characterized by the following two properties: 
*it is continuous with respect to the usual topologies on <math>\operatorname{Val}</math> and <math>\operatorname{Val}^\infty.</math>
* if <math>\phi=\operatorname{vol}_V(\bullet + A)</math> and <math>\psi= \operatorname{vol}_W(\bullet + B)</math> where <math>A\in \mathcal K(V)</math> and <math>B\in \mathcal K(W)</math> are convex bodies with smooth boundary and strictly positive Gauss curvature, and <math>\operatorname{vol}_V</math> and <math>\operatorname{vol}_W</math> are densities on <math>V</math> and <math>W,</math> then 
<math  display="block"> \phi\boxtimes \psi = (\operatorname{vol}_V\boxtimes \operatorname{vol}_W) (\bullet + A\times B).</math>

===Product===
The product of two smooth valuations <math>\phi,\psi\in\operatorname{Val}^\infty (V)</math> is defined by 
<math display=block> (\phi\cdot \psi)(K)= (\phi\boxtimes \psi)(\Delta(K)),</math>
where <math>\Delta : V\to V\times V</math> is the diagonal embedding. The product is a continuous map 
<math display=block> \operatorname{Val}^\infty (V) \times  \operatorname{Val}^\infty (V)  \to  \operatorname{Val}^\infty (V) .</math>
Equipped with this product, <math> \operatorname{Val}^\infty (V) </math> becomes a commutative associative graded algebra with the Euler characteristic as the multiplicative identity.

===Alesker-Poincaré duality===
By a theorem of Alesker, the restriction of the product 
<math display=block>\operatorname{Val}_k^\infty(V)\times \operatorname{Val}_{n-k}^\infty(V)\to \operatorname{Val}_n^\infty(V)=\operatorname{Dens}(V)</math> is a non-degenerate pairing. This motivates the definition of the <math>k</math>-homogeneous ''generalized valuation'', denoted <math>\operatorname{Val}_k^{-\infty}(V),</math> as <math>\operatorname{Val}^\infty_{n-k}(V)^*\otimes\operatorname{Dens}(V),</math> topologized with the weak topology. By the Alesker-Poincaré duality, there is a natural dense inclusion <math>\operatorname{Val}_k^\infty(V)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Val}_k^{-\infty}(V)/</math>

===Convolution===
Convolution is a natural product on <math>\operatorname{Val}^\infty(V)\otimes \operatorname{Dens}(V^*).</math> For simplicity, we fix a density <math>\operatorname{vol}</math> on <math>V</math> to trivialize the second factor. Define for fixed <math>A,B\in\mathcal K(V)</math> with smooth boundary and strictly positive Gauss curvature 
<math display=block>\operatorname{vol}(\bullet+A)\ast\operatorname{vol}(\bullet+B)=\operatorname{vol}(\bullet+A+B).</math> There is then a unique extension by continuity to a map 
<math display=block> \operatorname{Val}^\infty (V) \times  \operatorname{Val}^\infty (V)  \to  \operatorname{Val}^\infty (V),</math> called the convolution.
Unlike the product, convolution respects the co-grading, namely if <math>\phi\in\operatorname{Val}^\infty_{n-i}(V),</math> <math>\psi\in\operatorname{Val}^\infty_{n-j}(V),</math> then <math>\phi\ast\psi\in \operatorname{Val}^\infty_{n-i-j}(V).</math>

For instance, let <math>V(K_1,\ldots, K_n)</math> denote the mixed volume of the convex bodies <math>K_1,\ldots, K_n\subset \R^n.</math> If convex bodies <math>A_1,\dots,A_{n-i}</math> in <math>\R^n</math> with  a smooth boundary and strictly positive Gauss curvature   are fixed, then 
<math> \phi(K) = V(K[i], A_1,\dots,A_{n-i})</math>
defines a smooth valuation of degree <math>i.</math> The convolution two such valuations is
<math display=block>V(\bullet[i], A_1,\dots,A_{n-i})\ast V(\bullet[j],B_1,\dots,B_{n-j})=c_{i,j}V(\bullet[n-j-i], A_1,\dots,A_{n-i},B_1,\dots,B_{n-j}),</math>
where <math>c_{i,j}</math> is a constant depending only on <math>i,j,n.</math>

===Fourier transform===
The Alesker-Fourier transform is a natural, <math>GL(V)</math>-equivariant isomorphism of complex-valued valuations 
<math  display="block">\mathbb F: \operatorname{Val}^\infty(V)\to \operatorname{Val}^\infty(V^*)\otimes \operatorname{Dens}(V),</math> discovered by Alesker and enjoying many properties resembling the classical Fourier transform, which explains its name.

It reverses the grading, namely <math>\mathbb F: \operatorname{Val}_k^\infty(V) \to \operatorname{Val}^\infty_{n-k}(V^*)\otimes \operatorname{Dens}(V),</math> and intertwines the product and the convolution: <math display=block>\mathbb F(\phi\cdot \psi) = \mathbb F\phi\ast\mathbb F\psi.</math>

Fixing for simplicity a Euclidean structure to identify <math>V = V^*,</math> <math>\operatorname{Dens}(V)=\Complex,</math> we have the identity <math display=block>\mathbb F^2\phi(K) = \phi(-K).</math> On even valuations, there is a simple description of the Fourier transform in terms of the Klain embedding: <math>\operatorname{Kl}_{\mathbb F\phi}(E) = \operatorname{Kl}_\phi(E^\perp).</math> In particular, even real-valued valuations remain real-valued after the Fourier transform.

For odd valuations, the description of the Fourier transform is substantially more involved. Unlike the even case, it is no longer of purely geometric nature. For instance, the space of real-valued odd valuations is not preserved.

===Pullback and pushforward===
Given a linear map <math>f:U\to V,</math> there are induced operations of pullback <math>f^*:\operatorname{Val}(V)\to \operatorname{Val}(U)</math> and pushforward <math>f_*:\operatorname{Val}(U)\otimes\operatorname{Dens}(U)^*\to \operatorname{Val}(V)\otimes \operatorname{Dens}(V)^*.</math> The pullback is the simpler of the two, given by <math>f^*\phi(K)=\phi(f(K)).</math> It evidently preserves the parity and degree of homogeneity of a valuation.  
Note that the pullback does not preserve smoothness when <math>f</math> is not injective.

The pushforward is harder to define formally. For simplicity, fix Lebesgue measures on <math>U</math> and <math>V.</math> The pushforward can be uniquely characterized by describing its action on valuations of the form <math>\operatorname{vol}(\bullet+A),</math> for all <math>A\in \mathcal K(U),</math> and then extended by continuity to all valuations using the Irreducibility Theorem. For a surjective map <math>f,</math> 
<math display=block>f_*\operatorname{vol}(\bullet+A)=\operatorname{vol}(\bullet+f(A)).</math> For an inclusion <math>f:U\hookrightarrow V,</math> choose a splitting <math>V=U\oplus W.</math> Then 
<math display=block> f_*\operatorname{vol}(\bullet + A) (K)= \int_{W}\operatorname{vol}(K\cap (U+w) + A) dw.</math>
Informally, the pushforward is dual to the pullback with respect to the Alesker-Poincaré pairing: for <math>\phi\in \operatorname{Val}(V)</math> and <math>\psi\in\operatorname{Val}(U)\otimes\operatorname{Dens}(U)^*,</math> 
<math display=block>\langle f^*\phi,\psi\rangle =\langle \phi, f_*\psi\rangle.</math>
However, this identity has to be carefully interpreted since the pairing is only well-defined for smooth valuations. For further details, see.<ref name="Alesker:Fourier">{{citation
| last1=Alesker | first1=Semyon
| title=A Fourier-type transform on translation-invariant valuations on convex sets
| journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]
| volume=181
| date=2011
| pages=189–294
| doi=10.1007/s11856-011-0008-6| doi-access=free| arxiv=math/0702842
}}</ref>

==Valuations on manifolds==
In a series of papers beginning in 2006, Alesker laid down the foundations for a theory of valuations on manifolds that extends the theory of valuations on convex bodies. The key observation leading to this extension is that  via integration over the normal cycle ({{EquationNote|1}}), a smooth translation-invariant valuation may be evaluated on  sets  much more general than convex ones. Also ({{EquationNote|1}}) suggests to define  smooth valuations in general by dropping the requirement that the form <math>\omega</math> be translation-invariant and by replacing the translation-invariant Lebesgue measure with an arbitrary smooth measure.

Let <math>X</math> be an n-dimensional smooth manifold and let <math>\mathbb P_X= \mathbb P_+(T^* X)</math> be the co-sphere bundle of <math>X,</math> that is, the oriented projectivization of the cotangent bundle. 
Let <math>\mathcal P(X)</math> denote the collection of compact differentiable polyhedra in <math>X.</math>  The normal cycle <math>N(A)\subset \mathbb P_X</math> of <math>A\in \mathcal P(X),</math> which consists of the outward co-normals to <math>A,</math> is naturally a Lipschitz submanifold of dimension <math>n-1.</math>

For ease of presentation we henceforth assume that <math>X</math> is oriented, even though the concept of smooth valuations in fact does not depend on orientability.  The space of smooth valuations <math>\mathcal V^\infty(X)</math> on <math>X</math> consists of functions <math>\phi : \mathcal P(X)\to \Complex</math> of the form
<math display=block> \phi(A)= \int_A\mu + \int_{N(A)}\omega,\qquad A\in \mathcal P(X),</math>
where <math>\mu\in\Omega^n(X)</math> and <math>\omega\in \Omega^{n-1}(\mathbb P_X)</math> can be arbitrary. 
It was shown by Alesker that the smooth valuations on open subsets of <math>X</math> form a soft sheaf over <math>X.</math>

===Examples=== 
The following are examples of smooth valuations on a smooth manifold <math>X</math>:
* Smooth measures on <math>X.</math>
* The [[Euler characteristic]]; this follows from the work of [[Shiing-Shen Chern|Chern]]<ref>{{citation
| last1=Chern | first1=Shiing-Shen | authorlink1=Shiing-Shen Chern
| title=On the curvatura integra in a Riemannian manifold
| journal=Annals of Mathematics |series=Second Series
| volume=46
| year=1945
| issue=4 | pages=674–684
| doi=10.2307/1969203| jstor=1969203 | s2cid=123348816 }}</ref> on the [[Gauss-Bonnet theorem]], where such <math>\mu</math> and <math>\omega</math>  were constructed to represent the Euler characteristic. In particular, <math>\mu</math> is then the [[Chern–Gauss–Bonnet theorem|Chern-Gauss-Bonnet integrand]], which is the Pfaffian of the Riemannian curvature tensor.
* If <math>X</math> is Riemannian, then the Lipschitz-Killing valuations or intrinsic volumes <math>V_0^X = \chi, V_1^X, \ldots, V_n^X = \mathrm{vol}_X</math> are smooth valuations. If <math>f : X \to \R^m</math> is any [[Embedding|isometric immersion]] into a Euclidean space, then <math>V_i^X = f^* V_i^{\R^m},</math> where <math>V_i^{\R^m}</math> denotes the usual intrinsic volumes on <math>\R^m</math> (see below for the definition of the pullback).  The existence of these valuations is the essence of Weyl's tube formula.<ref>{{citation
| last1=Weyl | first1=Hermann
| title=On the Volume of Tubes
| journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics]]
| volume=61
| year=1939
| issue=2
| pages=461–472
| doi=10.2307/2371513| jstor=2371513
}}</ref>
* Let <math>\Complex P^n</math> be the [[complex projective space]], and let <math>\mathrm{Gr}_k^\Complex</math> denote the Grassmannian of all complex projective subspaces of fixed dimension <math>k.</math> The function 
<math display=block>\phi(A) = \int_{\mathrm{Gr}_k^\Complex} \chi(A\cap E) dE, \qquad A\in \mathcal P (\Complex P^n),</math> where the integration is with respect to the Haar probability measure on <math>\mathrm{Gr}_k^\Complex,</math> is a smooth valuation. This follows from the work of  Fu.<ref name="Fu:Kinematic">{{citation
| last1=Fu | first1=Joseph H. G.
| title=Kinematic formulas in integral geometry
| journal=Indiana University Mathematics Journal
| volume=39
| date=1990
| issue=4
| pages=1115–1154| doi=10.1512/iumj.1990.39.39052
| doi-access=free
}}</ref>

===Filtration===
The space <math>\mathcal V^\infty(X)</math> admits no natural grading in general, however it carries a canonical filtration 
<math display=block>\mathcal V^\infty(X) = W_0\supset W_1\supset \cdots \supset W_n.</math> Here <math>W_n</math> consists of the smooth measures on <math>X,</math> and <math>W_j</math> is given by forms <math>\omega</math> in the ideal generated by <math>\pi^*\Omega^j(X),</math> where <math>\pi : \mathbb P_X\to X</math> is the canonical projection.

The associated graded vector space <math>\bigoplus_{i=0}^n W_i/W_{i+1}</math> is canonically isomorphic to the space of smooth sections <math display=block>\bigoplus_{i=0}^n C^\infty (X, \operatorname{Val}_i^\infty(TX)),</math> where <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^\infty(TX)</math> denotes the vector bundle over <math>X</math> such that the fiber over a point <math>x\in X</math> is <math>\operatorname{Val}_i^\infty(T_x X),</math> the space of <math>i</math>-homogeneous smooth translation-invariant valuations on the tangent space <math>T_x X.</math>

===Product===
The space <math>\mathcal V^\infty(X)</math> admits a natural product. This product is continuous, commutative, associative, compatible with the filtration:
<math display=block> W_i\cdot W_j\subset W_{i+j},</math>
and has the Euler characteristic as the identity element. It also commutes with the restriction to embedded submanifolds, and the diffeomorphism group of <math>X</math> acts on <math>\mathcal V^\infty(X)</math> by algebra automorphisms.

For example, if <math>X</math> is Riemannian, the Lipschitz-Killing valuations satisfy 
<math display=block> V_i^X\cdot V_j^X= V_{i+j}^X.</math>

The Alesker-Poincaré duality still holds. For compact <math>X</math> it says that the pairing <math> \mathcal V^\infty(X)\times \mathcal V^\infty(X)\to \Complex,</math> <math>(\phi, \psi)\mapsto (\phi\cdot\psi) (X)</math> is non-degenerate. As in the translation-invariant case, this duality can be used to define generalized valuations. Unlike the translation-invariant case, no good definition of continuous valuations exists for valuations on manifolds.

The product of valuations closely reflects the geometric operation of intersection of subsets.
Informally, consider the generalized valuation <math>\chi_A=\chi(A\cap\bullet).</math> The product is given by <math>\chi_A\cdot\chi_B=\chi_{A\cap B}.</math> Now one can obtain smooth valuations by averaging generalized valuations of the form <math>\chi_A,</math> more precisely <math>\phi(X)=\int_S \chi_{s(A)}ds</math> is a smooth valuation if <math>S</math> is a sufficiently large measured family of diffeomorphisms. Then one has 
<math display=block>\int_S \chi_{s(A)}ds\cdot \int_{S'} \chi_{s'(B)}ds'=\int_{S\times S'} \chi_{s(A)\cap s'(B)}dsds',</math>
see.<ref>{{citation
| last1=Fu | first1=Joseph H. G.
| title=Intersection theory and the Alesker product
| journal=Indiana University Mathematics Journal
| volume=65
| date=2016
| issue=4
| pages=1347–1371| doi=10.1512/iumj.2016.65.5846
| arxiv=1408.4106
| s2cid=119736489
}}</ref>

===Pullback and pushforward===
Every smooth immersion <math>f : X \to Y</math> of smooth manifolds induces a pullback map <math>f^* : \mathcal V^\infty(Y) \to \mathcal V^\infty(X).</math> If <math>f</math> is an embedding, then 
<math display=block>(f^* \phi)(A) = \phi(f(A)), \qquad A\in\mathcal P (X).</math>
The pullback is a morphism of filtered algebras.
Every smooth proper submersion <math>f : X\to Y</math> defines a pushforward map <math>f_* : \mathcal V^\infty(X) \to \mathcal V^\infty(Y)</math> by 
<math display=block>(f_* \phi)(A) = \phi(f^{-1}(A)), \qquad A\in\mathcal P (Y).</math>  The pushforward is compatible with the filtration as well: <math>f_* : W_i(X)\to W_{i-(\dim X-\dim Y)}(Y).</math>
For general smooth maps, one can define pullback and pushforward for generalized valuations under some restrictions.

==Applications in Integral Geometry==
Let <math>M</math> be a [[Riemannian manifold]] and let <math>G</math> be a Lie group of isometries of <math>M</math> acting transitively on the sphere bundle <math>SM.</math> Under these assumptions the space <math>\mathcal V^\infty(M)^G</math> of <math>G</math>-invariant smooth valuations on <math>M</math> is finite-dimensional; let <math>\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_m</math> be a basis.  Let <math>A,B\in \mathcal P(M)</math> be differentiable polyhedra in <math>M.</math> Then integrals of the form <math>\int_G \phi_i(A\cap gB)dg</math> are expressible as linear combinations of <math>\phi_k(A)\phi_l(B)</math> with coefficients <math>c_i^{kl}</math> independent of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>: {{NumBlk|:|<math display=block> \int_G \phi_i(A\cap gB)dg = \sum_{k,l=1}^m c_i^{kl}  \phi_k(A)\phi_l(B),\qquad A,B \in \mathcal P(M).</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
Formulas of this type are called ''kinematic formulas''. Their existence in this generality was proved by Fu.<ref name="Fu:Kinematic"/> For the three simply connected real space forms, that is, the sphere, Euclidean space, and hyperbolic space, they go back to [[Wilhelm Blaschke|Blaschke]], [[Luis Santaló|Santaló]], [[Shiing-Shen Chern|Chern]], and  [[Herbert Federer|Federer]].

Describing the kinematic formulas explicitly  is typically a  difficult problem. In fact already in the step from real to complex space forms, considerable difficulties arise and these have  only recently been resolved  by Bernig, Fu, and  Solanes.<ref>{{citation
| last1=Bernig | first1=Andreas 
| last2=Fu | first2=Joseph H. G.
| last3=Solanes | first3=Gil
| title=Integral geometry of complex space forms
| journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]]
| volume=24
| year=2014
| issue=2
| pages=403–49
| doi=10.1007/s00039-014-0251-1 | doi-access=free| arxiv=1204.0604
}}2</ref>
<ref>{{citation
| last1=Bernig | first1=Andreas 
| last2=Fu|first2=Joseph H. G.
| title=Hermitian integral geometry
| journal=Annals of Mathematics |series=Second Series
| volume=173
| year=2011
| issue=2
| pages=907–945
| doi=10.4007/annals.2011.173.2.7| doi-access=free| arxiv=0801.0711
}}</ref> The key insight responsible for this progress is that the kinematic formulas contain the same information as the algebra of invariant valuations <math>\mathcal V^\infty(M)^G.</math> 
For a precise statement, let <math display=block>k_G : \mathcal V^\infty(M)^G \to \mathcal V^\infty(M)^G\otimes \mathcal V^\infty(M)^G</math>
be the kinematic operator, that is, the map determined by the kinematic formulas ({{EquationNote|2}}). Let 
<math display=block>\operatorname{pd} : \mathcal V^\infty(M)^G \to \mathcal V^\infty(M)^{G*}</math>
denote the Alesker-Poincaré duality, which is a linear isomorphism. Finally let <math>m_G^*</math> be the adjoint of the product map <math display=block>m_G : \mathcal V^\infty(M)^{G}\otimes \mathcal V^\infty(M)^{G}  \to \mathcal V^\infty(M)^{G}.</math> The Fundamental theorem of algebraic integral geometry relating operations on valuations to integral geometry, states that if the Poincaré duality is used to identify <math>\mathcal V^\infty(M)^{G}</math> with <math>\mathcal V^\infty(M)^{G*},</math> then <math>k_G=m_G^*</math>:

[[File:Fundamental theorem of algebraic integral geometry.svg|350px]].
